title: That Catchy Kars4Kids Jingle Might Disappear in California—Here's the Wild Reason Why
summary:
You know that super catchy song that goes "1-877-Kars4Kids, donate your car today"? It's been stuck in people's heads for 20 years. But now, a judge in California says the ad has to change—or go off the air there.

Why? Because the ad never explains where the money really goes. A man named Bruce Puterbaugh heard the jingle over and over and decided to donate his old Volvo. He thought the money would help needy kids in California. But he later found out most of it goes to a Jewish charity called Oorah, which runs summer camps and trips to Israel—mostly for Jewish families, not poor kids.

Bruce felt tricked. He said he never visited the website, where the charity does explain its mission. He just trusted the cute kids singing in the ad. So he sued.

In court, the judge heard that Oorah spent $16.5 million on a building in Israel and sent millions more to North Africa and the Middle East. The charity's own boss admitted the ad doesn't mention any of this.

The judge ruled the ad is "deceptive"—meaning it fools people. She ordered Kars4Kids to either add a clear message about its religious mission and where the money goes, or stop playing the ad in California. The charity says it will appeal, which means the fight isn't over.

So next time a jingle gets stuck in your head, remember: it's always smart to ask questions about where your money is really going.
why_it_matters: This matters because it shows why you should always look beyond catchy ads and ask where your donations or money really go before giving.

background_read: Kars4Kids is a real charity that has been using its famous jingle since 1999 to ask for car donations, and the ads have played on radio and TV many times.
In the United States, charities must follow truth-in-advertising rules, and California has especially strong laws to protect people from misleading ads.
The man who felt tricked, Bruce Puterbaugh, is a California resident who donated his car thinking the money would help local needy children.
Article_Structure: WHO: Bruce Puterbaugh, a man from California who donated his car, and the charity Kars4Kids.
WHAT: A judge ruled that the Kars4Kids jingle is deceptive because it doesn't explain that most money goes to a Jewish charity called Oorah.
WHERE: In California, where the ad was played and the lawsuit was filed.
WHY: Because Bruce felt tricked when he learned his donation didn't help poor kids in California as he expected.

perspectives.description: Some people think Kars4Kids does good work by running summer camps and cultural programs for Jewish families, and they support the charity's mission.
Others, like Bruce, feel disappointed because the ad didn't make it clear that the money isn't for all needy kids, which can break trust.
Legal experts say the court ruling is a reminder that all charities need to be truthful in their ads, no matter how catchy the music is.
